A missed lead change looks like a training problem. Nine times out of ten, Dr. Leo finds a loin or SI restriction that's been building for months.

The horse isn't being hard-headed. He literally cannot engage his hindquarters the way you're asking — and the more you drill it, the more he braces against the pain.

Three things North Texas riders notice first:
— He swaps late or not at all, especially going right.
— Ears back, tail wringing when you cue the transition.
— Drifting wide instead of collecting into the corner.

One adjustment doesn't fix years of compensation, but it does take the pain out of the equation so the training can actually stick.

If this sounds like your horse, DM us to book with Dr. Leo — we're running DFW this week.

Box sour. Gate sour. Call it what you want — most of the time it starts with a horse that hurts when he collects and stops hard.

One of our North Texas clients said it best after Dr. Leo worked her rope horse: "He doesn't dread the box anymore. That told me everything."

Attitude in the setup is data. A horse that tucks his head, locks up, or refuses to square is communicating — not acting out.

If your horse has been telling you something and you're not sure what to do next, start with a chiropractic exam.

You're hauling. You're running. You're doing everything right.

But by mid-summer, most performance horses in North Texas are carrying compensation patterns they picked up in May — and the body gets good at hiding them until it can't anymore.

A maintenance adjustment isn't a sign something is wrong. It's how serious competitors keep something from going wrong.
